lessons.title: Four voices, one chord: the voice-leading rules that make a progression sound smooth
lessons.explanation: Lesson 34 built triads from a key and lesson 41 gave each chord a function, but a chord symbol says nothing about which note goes in which octave or which voice takes it. Four-part writing, the soprano, alto, tenor and bass layout that Open Music Theory calls SATB style, is the smallest laboratory in which those decisions can be made and heard. The textbooks set four vertical constraints and two horizontal ones. Vertically: every voice stays inside its range; soprano to alto and alto to tenor stay within an octave of each other while the bass may sit further below the tenor; the chord is complete, with doubling chosen in the order root, then fifth, then third; and no two voices move in parallel fifths, octaves, twelfths or unisons, since those are the same interval class and the textbook treats the compound forms as octave equivalents. Horizontally: the leading tone rises by step to the tonic and the chordal seventh falls by step. Those six rules are not etiquette. Each one protects a different thing the ear uses to separate lines: range protects the identity of a part, spacing protects the blend, doubling protects the weight of the root, and the motion rules protect independence. The reason to learn them on four voices rather than on a full score is that four is the smallest number in which every rule can be broken and every fault can be heard.
lessons.example: Harmonise C, F, G7, C in C major, one chord per bar, at 72 beats per minute, where a beat is 0.833 s, a 4/4 bar is 3.333 s and the progression lasts 13.333 s (computed). Begin with the soprano, because it is the line a listener follows, and let it rise by step: G4, A4, B4, C5. Now fill downwards and check each constraint. Bar one, C major: soprano G4, alto E4, tenor C4, bass C3. The root is doubled in tenor and bass, the fifth is in the soprano, the third in the alto, soprano to alto is a minor third and alto to tenor a major third, so the upper three sit well inside an octave. Bar two, F major: soprano A4, alto F4, tenor C4, bass F3. The soprano and alto rise by step, the tenor holds the common tone C, the bass falls a fifth, and the root is doubled in alto and bass. Bar three, G7: soprano B4, alto F4, tenor D4, bass G2. All four chord tones appear once, which is what a seventh chord needs; the alto F was prepared as the common tone in the previous bar and now falls to E in bar four, and the soprano B is the leading tone. Bar four, C major: soprano C5, alto E4, tenor C4, bass C3. The leading tone rises a semitone to C, the seventh falls a semitone to E, and the tonic is tripled with the fifth omitted, the standard licence at a final tonic. Run the horizontal check pair by pair: soprano and bass move from a twelfth to a tenth to a compound third to two octaves, never two perfect intervals in similar motion, and the inner pairs produce parallel thirds and sixths, which the textbook allows.
lessons.question: A learner harmonises G, C, D7, G at 76 beats per minute and writes the soprano and alto as F sharp5 and F sharp4 over the D7 chord, with both voices rising to G5 and G4 over the final chord. Using the doubling and motion rules, what is wrong and how long is the progression?
lessons.answer: The leading tone F sharp is doubled in two adjacent upper voices and both rise to G, which produces a doubled octave by similar motion; the alto should take A4 or D4 instead, and four bars at 76 beats per minute last 12.632 s
lessons.distractor: Nothing is wrong, because a doubled leading tone is acceptable in an inner voice and the two voices resolve correctly by semitone; four bars at 76 beats per minute last 12.632 s
lessons.correction: The resolution is correct in pitch and wrong in texture: two voices a semitone apart both rising to the same pitch class arrive at an octave, and the arrival is a parallel octave in all but name, exactly the doubled leading tone that four-part practice forbids. The fault is easy to miss because each line behaves well on its own, which is why the check is vertical before it is horizontal: count how many times the leading tone appears, then look at what the pair does next. Replacing the alto F sharp with A4 keeps the chord complete, since D7 is D, F sharp, A, C, and leaves the leading tone single in the soprano, where it can rise to G without colliding with anything. At 76 beats per minute a beat is 0.789 s and a 4/4 bar is 3.158 s, so four bars are 12.632 s.

depth.definitions: Voice leading is the choice of which pitch each voice takes and how each voice moves to the next chord. SATB names the four standard voices, soprano, alto, tenor and bass, and in analysis the label describes a texture rather than a choir. Doubling means giving one chord tone to more than one voice; omission means leaving a chord tone out. Spacing is the distance between adjacent voices, and a spacing error is soprano to alto or alto to tenor wider than an octave. Voice crossing puts a lower voice above a higher one; overlap lets a voice move beyond the previous pitch of its neighbour without actually crossing. The four types of motion are similar (same direction, different intervals), parallel (same direction, same interval), contrary (opposite directions) and oblique (one voice stationary). Tendency tones are the leading tone, which resolves up, and the chordal seventh, which resolves down. Prerequisites: triad construction and quality from lesson 34, Roman numeral function from lesson 41, inversion and bass position from lesson 57, and the applied chords of lesson 71, which are voiced by the same rules.
depth.mechanism: A parallel fifth is audible as a loss of independence because the upper voice becomes a fixed harmonic of the lower one: at a 3:2 ratio the top note is the third partial of the bottom note, so the pair fuses into a single thick line rather than two lines. Parallel octaves are the extreme case, since a 2:1 ratio makes the upper voice the second partial and the ear hears one pitch with a doubling. Contrary motion does the opposite: it separates the partial patterns and gives each voice a contour of its own, which is why the rules insist on contrary motion into perfect intervals. The doubling order follows from the same physics. The root reinforces the fundamental, the fifth reinforces the third partial, and the third, which is the fifth partial, is weakest and most colour-determining, so doubling the third weights the chord towards its mode and doubling the leading tone creates two voices with an obligation to resolve in the same direction. Spacing obeys the overtone series: intervals are wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, so close packing belongs in the middle of the texture.
depth.secondExample: Take a deceptive motion, G7 to A minor, in C major at 66 beats per minute, and the rules produce an answer that surprises learners. The leading tone B is in the soprano over G7, and the chord resolves to A minor, so the soprano rises to C rather than falling to A; the leading tone keeps its obligation even when the tonic does not arrive. The chordal seventh F falls to E, which is the fifth of A minor, and the bass falls a tone from G to A while the tenor moves from D to C. Every voice moves by step, the arrival is a first-inversion tonic with the third in the soprano, and the phrase sounds finished even though the expected tonic never came. Lesson 74 named this a deceptive cadence; the voice leading explains why it works, because the tendency tones resolve exactly as they would have done into C major. At 66 beats per minute a bar is 3.636 s, so the two-chord gesture occupies 7.273 s, and a listener hears the arrival as a substitution rather than as an error.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is checking only the outer voices. A learner scans soprano against bass, sees no parallel fifths, and hands in a setting whose alto and tenor move in parallel twelfths for three bars. The diagnostic is mechanical: list the six voice pairs in a fixed order, soprano to alto, soprano to tenor, soprano to bass, alto to tenor, alto to bass, tenor to bass, and for each pair name the interval in chord one and chord two before judging direction. A second error is doubling the leading tone in an inner voice on the theory that the rule applies only to the soprano; the rule applies to the pitch, not the part. A third is treating the chordal seventh as free because it is consonant with the fifth of the chord; it still resolves down by step, and a seventh that leaps is the most audible fault in an otherwise correct setting.
depth.application: Task in one sitting of about 25 minutes, with a keyboard or a guitar and no metronome needed until the last step. Choose a four-chord progression you already play, such as C, A minor, F, G7 in C major, and write the soprano line first on a single staff, stepwise where possible. Then add alto, tenor and bass in that order, checking each new voice against the ones already written rather than against the chord symbol. Write the interval for all six pairs above each chord, and mark every motion as similar, parallel, contrary or oblique. Finally play the result at 72 beats per minute, sustaining each chord for a full bar, and listen for the one place where a voice jumps further than a third. Model answer for C, A minor, F, G7: soprano E5, E5, F5, D5; alto C5, C5, C5, B4; tenor G4, A4, A4, G4; bass C3, A2, F2, G2. Self-review rubric: one point for every voice inside its range, one for correct doubling in all four chords, one for a clean parallel scan, one for naming the tendency-tone resolutions aloud. Warm up before playing, keep the session under half an hour, and stop if a wrist or forearm aches rather than pushing through a repeated shape.
depth.summary: Four-part writing turns a chord symbol into four decisions: which pitch, which octave, which voice, and where each voice goes next. Ranges and spacing control the blend, doubling controls the weight, and contrary motion into perfect intervals plus the two tendency-tone resolutions control independence. The rules survive outside the chorale: any arrangement for voice and three instruments is solving the same problem, and a bass line, a chord part and a melody that all satisfy these constraints will sit together without EQ.

steps: Label the four rows from top to bottom as soprano, alto, tenor and bass, and write the voice ranges at the left edge: soprano C4 to A5, alto G3 to E5, tenor C3 to A4, bass E2 to E4.

Fill column three, G7, as B4, F4, D4 and G2, and label the two tendency tones in bold: B is the leading tone and F is the chordal seventh, prepared by the common tone from the previous column.

Fill column four, C major, as C5, E4, C4 and C3, and draw the two resolving arrows: B4 up a semitone to C5 and F4 down a semitone to E4, with the caption noting that the tonic is tripled and the fifth omitted at the final chord.

lessons.title: Non-chord tones: passing, neighbour, suspension and appoggiatura, and what each does to a phrase
lessons.explanation: Every note in a melody is either a chord tone or a non-chord tone, and the second category is where expression lives. Open Music Theory calls these embellishing tones and treats them as the melodic layer above a harmonic skeleton; Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom separates them by how they are approached and left, which is the only test that works reliably. A passing tone is approached by step and left by step in the same direction, filling a third. A neighbour tone is approached by step and returns to the same pitch, upper or lower. An escape tone is approached by leap and left by step in the opposite direction. An appoggiatura is approached by leap and resolved by step, usually in the same direction as the leap or downwards, and it is normally accented. A suspension is prepared on the same pitch, held as a dissonance on a strong beat and resolved down by step, and it is named by the interval pair against the bass, so 4-3 means a fourth resolving to a third. An anticipation arrives early, stating the next chord's note before the chord does. Two variables decide all of it: the approach, meaning what the previous note was and how the voice got there, and the metric position, meaning whether the note falls on a beat the ear is counting.
lessons.example: Label a four-bar melody over C, A minor, F, G7 at 84 beats per minute, where a beat is 0.714 s, a bar is 2.857 s and the phrase is 11.429 s (computed). Bar one, over C: E4 for two beats as the third of the chord, F4 on beat three as a passing tone between E4 and G4, then G4 on beat four as the fifth. Bar two, over A minor: A4 for two beats as the root, B4 as an eighth-note upper neighbour on beat three, A4 again as its return, then C5 on beat four as the third. Bar three, over F: A4 on beat one as the third, a leap up to D5 on beat two, which is an appoggiatura because it is reached by leap and resolves down by step to C5 on beat three, with C5 held through beat four as the fifth. Bar four, over G7: the same C5 is tied into beat one, where it is now a fourth above the bass G and therefore a 4-3 suspension, resolving down by step to B4 on beat two, then A4 on beat three as a passing tone on the way to G4, the root, on beat four. Count the result: fifteen melodic events, of which five are non-chord tones, so the ratio is 33.3 per cent (computed). That ratio is normal for a tonal melody; a line with no non-chord tones sounds like an arpeggio exercise, and a line where half the notes are foreign stops implying a harmony at all.
lessons.question: A singer holds C5 across the bar line while the band changes from F to G7, then falls to B4 on beat two. Later the same singer arrives at C5 a beat early, on beat four of the G7 bar, and holds it into the C chord. A learner labels both notes suspensions. Which label is right, and what distinguishes them?
lessons.answer: Only the first is a suspension, prepared on the same pitch and resolved down by step on a strong beat; the second is an anticipation, because it states the next chord's note before the chord arrives
lessons.distractor: Both are suspensions, because each is a held note that resolves by step and each is consonant with the chord that follows it
lessons.correction: A suspension is defined by three stages in order: preparation as a consonance, dissonance on a strong beat, and resolution down by step, and its identity comes from the interval against the bass, which here is a fourth falling to a third. An anticipation reverses the timing: the note that belongs to the next chord sounds before that chord begins, so it is dissonant against the chord still in force and consonant once the harmony changes. The two are mirror images, one delaying a chord tone and the other arriving early, and telling them apart needs only the position of the bar line. Both feel like expressive devices, which is why the labels get confused, but only the suspension is an accented dissonance that must resolve; an anticipation has nothing to resolve because the resolution is the chord change itself.

depth.definitions: A chord tone belongs to the harmony in force at that moment; a non-chord tone does not. Approach and departure are the two neighbouring notes, and their intervals and directions classify the tone. Passing tones fill a third by step; neighbour tones return to the pitch they left; escape tones are leapt into and stepped out of in the opposite direction; appoggiaturas are leapt into and resolved by step, usually accented; suspensions are held over from the previous chord and resolve down by step, named 9-8, 7-6, 4-3, 2-3 or 6-5 against the bass; retardations are the same device resolving upwards; anticipations arrive early; pedal points hold one pitch through changing harmony. Accented means on a beat or a strong subdivision, unaccented means between beats. Prerequisites: chord tones from lesson 34, Roman numerals from lesson 41, cadence types from lesson 74, melody writing from lesson 46, and the four-part setting of lesson 81, where suspensions first appear as vertical events.
depth.mechanism: The ear assigns a note to the harmony or to the melody according to two cues: metric weight and the size of the interval moved. A note on a strong beat is heard as part of the harmony unless it is prepared and resolved in a way that marks it as decoration, which is why a suspension, the one accented dissonance that is both prepared and stepwise, sounds expressive rather than wrong. A note between beats is heard as motion, so a passing tone or a neighbour barely registers as dissonance at all. That is also why the same pitch changes status when the chord changes: G is the fifth of C, the seventh of A minor, the ninth of F and the root of G7, so a held G moves from consonance to dissonance without the singer doing anything. The practical consequence is that melodic analysis cannot be done without the harmony underneath, and harmonic analysis cannot ignore which notes are structural, which is the point Open Music Theory makes when it separates the embellishing layer from the framework.
depth.secondExample: Take a ii to V to I in F major at 92 beats per minute, where a bar is 2.609 s, and put the anticipation at the end of the dominant. Over G minor the melody moves F4, E4, D4; over C7 it moves E4, D4, C4 with C4 as the seventh; then, on beat four of the C7 bar, the singer states F4, which belongs to the F chord that has not yet arrived. That F4 is an anticipation, dissonant against C7 and consonant a beat later, and it is the single most common non-chord tone in gospel and soul singing. Now delay the same arrival instead: hold G4 from the C7 bar into the F bar and resolve it to F4 on beat two, and the device becomes a 9-8 suspension, prepared, accented and resolved down by step. The two versions last the same 2.609 s bar and use the same two pitches, and they feel completely different, one pushing forward and one leaning back, which is the difference between arriving early and arriving late.
depth.mistake: The standard error is classifying by shape rather than by approach: a learner sees a note that is not in the chord and writes passing tone for all of them, then cannot explain why the phrase sounds the way it does. The diagnostic is a three-question routine applied to each note: is the previous note the same pitch, a step away or a leap away; is the next note a step or a leap; and is the note on a beat or between beats. A second error is treating a suspension as an appoggiatura because both resolve down by step, when the difference is the preparation on the same pitch. A third, common in production, is quantising a performance so that every resolution lands exactly on the beat, which removes the leaning quality that made the phrase expressive; the correction is to keep the note start slightly late rather than to move the chord.
depth.application: Task over two sittings of 20 minutes, the first at a desk and the second with an instrument or in a DAW. Choose eight bars of a song whose chords you know, write the chord symbols above the staff, and label every note as a chord tone or with one of the six non-chord tone names. Count the ratio of non-chord tones to total events and compare it with the 33.3 per cent of the worked example. Then rewrite the melody twice: once with every non-chord tone removed, so only chord tones remain, and once with an anticipation added before each chord change. Play or sequence all three versions and write one sentence on which one sounds like a melody and which sounds like an exercise. Model answer for the example phrase: five non-chord tones in fifteen events, one passing tone in bar one, one upper neighbour in bar two, one appoggiatura and one suspension in bars three and four, and one passing tone in bar four. Self-review rubric: one point for using approach and departure rather than shape, one for naming the metric position of each tone, one for a ratio computed rather than estimated, one for the written comparison of the three versions. Warm up before playing, keep the instrument at a comfortable volume, and stop if a hand or wrist aches.
depth.summary: Non-chord tones are classified by how they are approached, how they are left and where they sit in the bar. Passing and neighbour tones decorate motion, the escape tone decorates a leap, the appoggiatura makes an accented dissonance out of a leap, the suspension delays a chord tone that was already sounding, and the anticipation states one early. The same pitch can be a chord tone in one bar and a dissonance in the next, so the labels only mean anything against a harmony and a metre.

lessons.title: Write a countermelody: contrary motion, strong-beat consonance and the crossing test
lessons.explanation: Lesson 81 arranged four voices under one chord; this lesson writes a second line that is meant to be heard as a line in its own right. The grammar comes from species counterpoint, which is not a historical curiosity but the cheapest available test of whether two melodies can coexist. The rules that matter are few. Begin and end on an octave or a unison. On each strong beat the interval between the lines must be consonant: unisons, thirds, fifths, sixths and their compounds are consonant, while seconds, fourths and sevenths are not, with the fourth treated as dissonant when it is measured against the lowest voice. Imperfect consonances, the third and the sixth, may be approached by any motion, but no more than three consecutive thirds or sixths are allowed, because four in a row stop sounding like two lines and start sounding like one line doubled. Perfect consonances, the unison, fifth, octave and twelfth, must be approached by contrary motion, which is what prevents the direct fifth and direct octave. A melody may leap only a third, fourth, fifth, ascending minor sixth or octave, and after a leap it should change direction. Finally, the ending is approached by contrary motion, with the upper line moving 7 to 8 and the lower moving 2 to 1, which in a mode such as G Mixolydian or D Dorian needs an added sharp to supply the leading tone.
lessons.example: Write a countermelody above an eight-note cantus firmus in G major at 60 beats per minute, where each whole note lasts a 4 s bar and the exercise lasts 32.0 s (computed). The cantus is G4, A4, B4, C5, D5, B4, A4, G4. Begin the counter on G5, an octave above, and choose each next note so that the strong-beat interval stays consonant and the motion stays contrary where possible. The result is G5, F sharp5, D5, A5, F sharp5, D5, F sharp5, G5. Check it bar by bar: octave, major sixth, minor third, major sixth, major third, minor third, major sixth, octave. Every interval is consonant, and no more than two thirds occur in a row, since bars five and six are thirds and bar seven is a sixth. Check the leaps: a semitone, a minor third, a perfect fifth upwards, a minor third down, a minor third, a minor third, a semitone. The fifth upward in bar four is followed by a change of direction, as the melodic rules require. Check the approach to the final octave: F sharp5 rises a semitone to G5 while A4 falls a tone to G4, so the motion is contrary and the two lines supply 7 to 8 above and 2 to 1 below. The counter is not a harmonisation of the cantus; it is a melody that could be sung alone, and the test is whether its own contour makes sense with the cantus removed.
lessons.question: A learner writes a countermelody below a tune in A minor and, at the chorus, the lower line rises to E5 while the tune sits on C5, then both lines descend in parallel fifths for two bars. What are the two faults and what should replace them?
lessons.answer: The lower line has crossed above the tune, which ends its identity as a lower voice, and the parallel fifths destroy the independence of the lines; the counter should stay below and move to a third or sixth under C5 on that beat, with contrary motion taking it away from the next perfect interval
lessons.distractor: Neither is a fault, because the interval of a tenth is consonant and parallel fifths are permitted when the upper line moves by step
lessons.correction: A voice that crosses above the part it is supposed to be under stops being heard as that part, which is why the crossing test comes before any interval check; the ear tracks register as identity. Parallel fifths are the textbook example of lost independence at any speed, and the fact that the upper line moves by step makes them smoother and therefore harder to notice, not permissible. The repair is to choose the pitch on the strong beat that gives a third or a sixth under the tune, then to move the counter by step or third into the following bar so that the next perfect interval, if there is one, is approached by contrary motion. Both faults are audible in a two-bar loop, which is why the check is worth running before the line is learned.

depth.definitions: A countermelody is a second melodic line written to be heard alongside a principal melody, distinct from a chordal accompaniment because it has its own contour and rhythm. A cantus firmus is the given melody in a counterpoint exercise. Species counterpoint is a teaching method in which the rhythm of the added line is fixed, note against note in first species, two notes against one in second species, four in third, suspensions in fourth and a mixture in fifth. Consonances are the unison, third, fifth, sixth and octave with their compounds; dissonances are the second, fourth, seventh and their compounds, with the fourth context-dependent. Direct or hidden fifths and octaves occur when similar motion approaches a perfect interval; parallel motion keeps the same interval class. Voice crossing puts the lower part above the upper. Prerequisites: interval quality from lesson 32, triads and their doubling from lesson 34, the four-part rules of lesson 81, and the modal colour of lesson 73, which explains why a mode may need an added leading tone at the close.
depth.mechanism: Two lines are heard as independent when they differ in at least two of three properties: contour, rhythm and register. Contrary motion separates contour, so the ear can follow either line without confusion; similar motion in the same interval class fuses them, because the upper voice keeps a constant relationship to the lower one and stops carrying new information. That is why the rule permits parallel thirds and sixths briefly but forbids four in a row: imperfect consonances blur slowly, perfect ones blur at once. The rhythmic dimension works the same way, and this is where a countermelody differs from a chord part. If the counter moves when the tune holds and holds when the tune moves, the two lines interlock; if both move together, the result is homophony no matter how independent the pitches look on paper. The best practical test is to sing the counter alone and then with the tune, and to notice whether either line becomes hard to follow.
depth.secondExample: Take a pop chorus in A minor at 104 beats per minute, where a bar is 2.308 s, with a vocal on A4, C5, B4, A4 and a bass guitar written as the counter line. On the first beat the bass plays A2 under A4, which is two octaves, and on beat three it falls to F2 while the vocal rises to C5, so the interval opens from an octave to a compound fifth and the motion is contrary. In bar two the vocal falls to B4 and the bass rises to G2, giving a compound third, then both settle on A. The bass is a countermelody in the useful sense because it has its own contour, falls when the voice rises, and lands consonant intervals on the strong beats. Note what happens if the same bass is written an octave higher and played on the guitar's lower strings: the intervals are the same class but the register collapses into the vocal, and the crossing test fails even though every interval on paper is legal. Register is part of the rule, not a mixing preference.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is writing the counter as a shadow: a third or a sixth below the tune for every note, which is consonant everywhere and sounds like a doubled melody with a strange tone. The diagnostic is to count the motion types across the passage; if every bar uses similar or parallel motion, the line is a doubling rather than a counterpoint. A second error is repairing a dissonance by changing the chord underneath instead of the line, which is easy in a DAW and hides the fault, because the exercise is about two melodies that must work against a given harmony. A third is ignoring the melodic rules for the added line itself: repeated notes, a leap followed by a leap in the same direction, or an outline of a tritone, any of which makes a technically consonant line impossible to sing.
depth.application: Task in two sessions of 20 minutes, one at a desk and one at an instrument. Take an eight-bar melody you already play and write a countermelody below it, beginning and ending on an octave or unison, with consonant intervals on every strong beat and at least one bar of contrary motion per two bars. Write the interval above each strong beat and the motion type between bars. Then play the tune alone, the counter alone, and both together, and ask a listener which of the two lines they could hum back. Model answer for the G major cantus in the example: intervals octave, sixth, third, sixth, third, third, sixth, octave; leaps of a semitone, third, fifth, third, third, third, semitone; motion contrary into the final octave with 7 to 8 above and 2 to 1 below. Self-review rubric: one point for beginning and ending correctly, one for consonant strong beats throughout, one for no more than three consecutive imperfect consonances, one for a written sentence on which version was easier to follow. Keep the instrument at a comfortable level, warm up first, and stop if the fretting hand aches during repeated shapes.
depth.summary: A countermelody is a second line with its own contour, rhythm and register, tested bar by bar for consonance on strong beats and for motion that separates it from the tune. Begin and end on an octave or unison, approach perfect intervals by contrary motion, cap the consecutive thirds and sixths at three, and keep the leaps singable. The same tests decide whether a bass line, a synth lead or a horn part is a real second voice or merely a doubling.

visual.title: Eight-bar cantus firmus with a countermelody above: interval labels and motion arrows - reasoning sequence
visual.description: Two staves, cantus firmus below and counter above, one whole note per bar for eight bars, with the interval name written between the staves, a motion arrow beside each bar, and the leap sizes of the counter noted above its staff.
steps: Label eight bars one to eight, place the cantus firmus in whole notes on the lower staff as G4, A4, B4, C5, D5, B4, A4, G4, and write the tempo 60 above bar one.

Write the interval between the staves for each bar: octave, major sixth, minor third, major sixth, major third, minor third, major sixth, octave, and circle the two bars of consecutive thirds as the limit case.
Draw a motion arrow at each bar line labelled contrary, similar or oblique, and mark bar four, where the counter leaps a fifth upward, with a note that the direction changes in the next bar.

Annotate the last bar: the arrow from F sharp5 to G5 labelled 7 to 8, the arrow from A4 to G4 labelled 2 to 1, and the caption noting that the two arrows point in opposite directions, which is what makes the final octave legal.

lessons.title: Harmonic rhythm: how often the chord changes decides how the phrase feels
lessons.explanation: Harmonic rhythm is the term for how long each chord lasts, and it is the parameter learners most often change without knowing they have changed it. Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom defines it exactly that way and then compares real repertoire: in one group of songs each chord lasts four beats and the harmonic rhythm is described as whole-note, while in a Mozart example and a Wagner example each chord lasts two beats and the harmonic rhythm is faster. Two consequences follow. First, harmonic rhythm is independent of tempo in principle and linked to it in practice, because what a listener perceives is the duration of each chord in seconds, not the number of chords per bar. Second, harmonic rhythm is a formal device: a phrase that doubles its chord rate is accelerating even if the drummer does not change, and a phrase that halves it is broadening, which is why the last two bars before a cadence so often hold one chord. Hypermeter extends the same logic above the bar, grouping bars into pairs and fours, and a chord change that contradicts the four-bar grouping is heard as a syncopation at the level of the phrase rather than the beat.
lessons.example: Take an eight-bar phrase in C major at 100 beats per minute, where a beat is 0.6 s, a 4/4 bar is 2.4 s and the phrase is 19.2 s (computed), and set the same harmony three ways. Version one gives each chord one bar: C, A minor, F, G, C, A minor, D7, G7, so each chord lasts 2.4 s and the phrase contains eight harmonic events. Version two gives two chords per bar for the first six bars and one chord for the last two, so the rate doubles to 1.2 s per chord and then halves at the cadence, which is the standard acceleration into a close and the reason the arrival feels earned. Version three gives each chord two bars, so C lasts 4.8 s, F lasts 4.8 s, G7 lasts 4.8 s and the phrase contains four harmonic events in the same 19.2 s. Play all three at the same tempo and the tempo does not change, yet version two sounds impatient, version three sounds hymn-like, and version one sounds like a default. Now count what the ear is reacting to: eight events, fourteen events and four events in the same span, which is more than a threefold difference in event density with no change of beat.
lessons.question: A twelve-bar blues at 120 beats per minute uses one chord per bar with the quick change to IV in bar two. A revision holds the tonic for the first four bars instead. What are the durations, and what has the revision removed?
lessons.answer: Each bar lasts 2.0 s and the form lasts 24.0 s; the revision removes the harmonic marker that announces the start of the second phrase, so the phrase boundary must now be carried by the melody, the drums or the lyric
lessons.distractor: Each bar lasts 2.0 s and the form lasts 24.0 s; the revision changes nothing a listener can hear, because the same chords occupy the same total time either way
lessons.correction: The total time is identical, which is exactly why the change is easy to dismiss, but harmonic rhythm is about which harmony occupies the time, not only how much time there is. In the standard pattern the move to IV in bar two is what tells the ear that the first four-bar group has begun rather than merely continued, and that information disappears when bars one to four all sit on the tonic. The listener then relies on other cues, which is why a band can play the revised form successfully if the drummer marks the phrase and the lyric changes, and why the same revision sounds shapeless when nothing else marks the boundary. At 120 beats per minute a beat is 0.5 s, so a bar is 2.0 s, four bars are 8.0 s and the twelve-bar form is 24.0 s.

depth.definitions: Harmonic rhythm is the duration of each harmony, expressed in beats, bars or seconds. Rate is the number of chord changes per unit of time; acceleration shortens each chord, deceleration lengthens it. Static harmony holds one chord for a long span. Hypermeter groups bars into pairs, fours and eights, the way metre groups beats into bars. Phrase rhythm is the interaction between the phrase and that grouping. A syncopated harmonic change arrives before or after the strong point where the ear expects it. A cadence is the harmonic arrival that closes a phrase, and its weight depends on how long the dominant has been in place. Prerequisites: chord function from lesson 41, cadence types from lesson 74, phrase analysis from lesson 75, hypermetre and syncopation from lesson 53, and the chord chart reading of lesson 61, since a chart notates harmonic rhythm only by the spacing of its symbols.
depth.mechanism: The ear segments music into events and groups the events into phrases, and a chord change is one of the strongest event boundaries available. When the rate doubles, boundaries arrive twice as often, so the same melody feels more urgent even though nothing about the melody has changed; when the rate halves, each harmony occupies more time and the phrase feels broader. Duration also controls expectation, because a dominant that has lasted two bars has had time to create a stronger expectation than one that lasted half a bar, which is why the cadential dominant is often the longest chord in the phrase. Hypermeter adds a second layer: if the chord changes every two bars in a passage that has been changing every bar, the listener hears a slowing at the level of the phrase, not merely a different chord. None of this requires a listener to count; the effect is available to anyone who taps a foot, which is why producers reach for it when a chorus needs to lift without adding instruments.
depth.secondExample: Compare the blues pattern with a modal vamp, because the two use harmonic rhythm in opposite ways. A twelve-bar blues at 120 beats per minute has twelve events in 24.0 s, and the quick change in bar two adds a thirteenth decision by splitting the second bar into two harmonies of 1.0 s each, a doubling of the local rate that lasts only half a bar. A modal tune in D Dorian that holds D minor for eight bars at the same tempo has one event in 16.0 s, so the harmony supplies no boundaries at all and the form has to be carried by the riff, the drum pattern and the melody, which is why modal music so often has a memorable two-bar figure and an active drummer. Neither approach is more advanced; they place the information in different layers, and a piece that holds one chord for eight bars while also refusing to develop the riff simply stops moving.
depth.mistake: The most common error is to confuse harmonic rhythm with tempo. Adding chords to a bar does not speed the beat, and slowing the tempo does not make the harmony broader in the sense that matters, since a piece can be slow and busy or fast and static. The diagnostic is to count chord changes per phrase and separately to measure the phrase in seconds, then to describe each chord by its duration. A second error is the assumption that more chords mean more harmonic interest: substituting two chords for one often removes the contrast that made the original change mean something. A third is accidental syncopation, where a chord symbol is placed a beat early or late in a chart and the whole phrase shifts against the drums; the correction is to notate the change on the beat where it is played and to say so in the chart, because the spacing of symbols on a lead sheet is the only notation harmonic rhythm has.
depth.application: Task in one session of about 25 minutes, using a DAW or a keyboard and a stopwatch or the project tempo field. Choose an eight-bar progression you know, and write three versions: one chord per bar, two chords per bar, and one chord per two bars. Set the tempo to 100 beats per minute, which makes a bar 2.4 s, and play or sequence each version twice. For each, write down the duration of every chord in seconds and the number of harmonic events in the phrase. Then decide which version suits a verse, which suits a chorus, and which suits a final cadence, and write one sentence justifying each choice by duration rather than by taste. Model answer for the C major phrase: version one has eight events of 2.4 s; version two has fourteen events, twelve of 1.2 s and two of 2.4 s; version three has four events of 4.8 s; all three last 19.2 s. Self-review rubric: one point for correct arithmetic in all three versions, one for a written comparison of event counts, one for a cadence decision justified by the length of the dominant, one for noticing any chord that lands off the beat in your own chart. Keep monitoring levels low, take a break between versions, and stop if your hands or ears feel fatigued.
depth.summary: Harmonic rhythm is the duration of each chord, and it shapes a phrase as strongly as melody or tempo. Count events, convert them to seconds, and notice where the rate changes: acceleration pushes forward, deceleration broadens, and a long dominant is what makes an arrival feel earned. The device is available without adding a single instrument, which is why it is the first thing to change when a section needs to move differently.

readings.title: [110] Open Music Theory - Hypermeter

visual.title: One eight-bar phrase at three harmonic rhythms: a bar-by-bar block timeline - reasoning sequence
visual.description: Three parallel timelines of eight bars at 100 beats per minute, each bar 2.4 s wide, with chord blocks drawn to scale inside them so that a two-bar chord occupies twice the width of a one-bar chord.
steps: Draw eight equal bar boxes in a row and label them one to eight, then write the tempo and the arithmetic at the left margin: 100 beats per minute, beat 0.6 s, bar 2.4 s.
In the first timeline place eight blocks of equal width labelled C, A minor, F, G, C, A minor, D7, G7, and annotate each block with 2.4 s.

In the third timeline place four blocks spanning two bars each, labelled C, F, G7 and C, and annotate each with 4.8 s to show the halved rate.
Add a margin note under the third timeline stating that all three versions last 19.2 s, so the difference a listener hears is event density rather than total duration.

lessons.title: Texture: four ways to set the same harmony, from one line to four
lessons.explanation: Texture is the density of and the interaction between a work's voices, and the standard account divides it into four categories. Monophony is a single unaccompanied melodic line, even when several players perform it in unison. Heterophony is several simultaneous variants of one melodic line, the texture of much Turkish classical music and of a congregation singing a hymn with ornaments. Homophony is several voices moving together harmonically, and it splits into the homorhythmic kind, where every voice attacks at once, and the melody-and-accompaniment kind, where a tune is supported by chords. Polyphony is several melodic lines with independent rhythms. Two further devices sit alongside the categories rather than replacing them: an ostinato repeats a short figure underneath changing material, and call and response alternates a phrase between a leader and a group. What all of this describes is not the list of instruments but the number of independent things a listener can follow, which is why a four-piece band can be monophonic at one moment and polyphonic eight bars later without changing line-up.
lessons.example: Take a four-bar loop in C major at 92 beats per minute, where a beat is 0.652 s, a bar is 2.609 s and a sixteen-bar section is 41.739 s (computed), and set it four ways. Version one is a single guitar line playing the melody: monophony, four attacks in bar one, and nothing else to follow. Version two adds the same melody sung while the guitar strums block chords on every beat: eight chord attacks plus four melodic notes in bar one, all landing together, which is homorhythmic homophony. Version three keeps the chords but gives the bass a walking line in quarter notes and the vocal a syncopated phrase that crosses the bar line, so bar one now contains eight chord attacks, four bass notes and three vocal notes placed between them, which is polyphony because three rhythms are independent. Version four replaces the walking bass with a two-note ostinato that repeats every bar and lets the vocal answer the guitar in the gaps, which is call and response over an ostinato. The harmony is identical in all four versions and lasts the same 41.739 s per section; the density rises from four attacks per bar to fifteen or more, and what changes is how many events the ear must separate rather than how many notes exist.
lessons.question: A producer wanting a bigger chorus adds a pad playing the same chord rhythm as the guitar, doubles the vocal an octave up, and leaves the bass and drums unchanged. A learner describes the result as polyphonic. Is that right, and what actually changed?
lessons.answer: It is still homophony, because every added part attacks with the existing ones; density and register changed, but no new independent line or rhythm appeared
lessons.distractor: It is polyphonic, because the chord, the doubled vocal and the guitar are three different parts sounding at once, and any combination of simultaneous parts is polyphony
lessons.correction: The number of parts is not the test; independence is. A pad that duplicates the guitar's rhythm adds weight in the same frequency range and a vocal doubled an octave up adds a second register of the same line, so the listener still hears one harmonic gesture with a tune on top, which is homophony. Polyphony requires separate melodic lines and rhythms, and the practical consequence is that the chorus will sound louder and thicker but not more contrapuntal, and the added pad may mask the guitar because the two occupy the same register and the same attack times. To make the texture polyphonic, one part has to move when the others hold, which is a compositional decision rather than a mixing one.

depth.definitions: Texture is the density of and interaction between voices. A voice is any independent line, whether sung or played. Monophony is one unaccompanied line; heterophony is simultaneous variants of one line; homophony is voices moving harmonically together, either homorhythmically or as melody with accompaniment; polyphony is independent lines with independent rhythms. Density is the number of simultaneous events; registral spread is the distance between the lowest and highest sounding parts. An ostinato is a repeated figure, a riff is an ostinato with a rhythmic identity, and call and response alternates between leader and group. Doubling repeats a line at the unison or an octave, which thickens without adding independence. Prerequisites: layering and masking from lesson 39, rhythm section roles from lesson 45, the second-section writing of lesson 59, and the four-part spacing rules of lesson 81, since a chorale texture is homophony with strict voice leading.
depth.mechanism: A listener separates simultaneous sounds using onset time, register and timbre, and texture is the description of how those cues are distributed. Parts that attack together fuse into a single perceived event, which is why homorhythmic writing sounds like one block even with ten instruments. Parts that attack at different times remain separable, which is why a syncopated counterline is audible under a dense pad. Register matters because two parts in the same octave compete for the same critical bands and mask each other, while parts an octave or more apart stay distinct. This is the acoustic reason orchestration texts advise wide spacing low and denser packing in the middle: the ear has more room to separate events where the spectrum is less crowded. The practical consequence is that texture can be changed without adding or removing a single instrument, by changing when each part attacks.
depth.secondExample: A verse and a chorus can differ in texture with no change of line-up, and the effect is stronger than adding a synth. In the verse, let the vocal be accompanied only by a bass playing roots on the first beat of each bar and a muted guitar playing one chord per bar: two attacks per bar, a wide registral gap between the bass and the voice, and a texture close to monophony with punctuation. In the chorus, keep the same three players but give the guitar eighth-note chords, the bass a walking quarter-note line and the drummer a backbeat, so the same harmony now produces eight, four and two attacks per bar in three different rhythms. At 92 beats per minute each version lasts the same 2.609 s per bar, and the chorus will sound roughly twice as dense without a single new part being added. That is the cheapest lift available in arrangement, and it is also the reason a chorus that adds instruments without changing rhythms often fails to lift.
depth.mistake: The standard error is to use texture as a synonym for instrumentation, so a learner believes that adding a string pad has changed the texture from homophony to polyphony. The diagnostic is to count independent rhythms in a bar and to check whether any part moves while another holds; if every part attacks together, the texture is homophonic no matter how many parts there are. A second error is confusing texture with form: verse and chorus are sections, and each can be in any texture. A third, common in production, is thickening without separation, where three parts occupy the same octave and the same rhythm, so the mix gets louder and the arrangement gets no clearer; the fix is to move one part by an octave or to displace its attacks rather than to add EQ.
depth.application: Task in one session of 30 minutes with an instrument or a DAW, plus five minutes of listening. Choose a four-bar loop and produce it four times: as a single line, as that line with block chords, as the line with chords and an independent bass rhythm, and as the line with an ostinato and a call-and-response gap. For each version write down the number of attacks per bar, the number of independent rhythms, and the registral span in octaves. Then play the four versions to someone who has not heard them and ask which one they would call busy, and compare that answer with your counts. Model answer for the C major loop at 92 beats per minute: version one has four attacks per bar and one rhythm; version two has twelve attacks and one rhythm; version three has fifteen attacks and three rhythms; version four has twelve attacks and two rhythms plus a repeated figure. Self-review rubric: one point for counting attacks rather than instruments, one for naming the texture of each version, one for a written note on which version masked which part, one for a sentence on how you would make the fourth version polyphonic. Keep playback levels moderate, take breaks, and stop if your ears ring or your hands ache.
depth.summary: Texture describes how many independent things a listener can follow, not how many instruments are playing. Monophony, heterophony, homophony and polyphony are the four categories, with ostinato and call and response as devices that cut across them. Change the attacks, the register and the independence and the arrangement changes; add instruments without changing those and it only gets louder.

visual.title: Sixteen bars in four textures: an entry grid with attack counts - reasoning sequence
visual.description: A sixteen-bar grid at 92 beats per minute with four stacked rows labelled melody, chords, bass and vocal, each cell showing either a note event, a hold or a rest, with the number of attacks per bar written at the right edge of each row.
steps: Draw sixteen columns for the bars and label the tempo and the arithmetic at the left: 92 beats per minute, beat 0.652 s, bar 2.609 s, sixteen bars 41.739 s.
Fill version one as a single row of four attacks in each four-bar group, and write monophony and four attacks per bar beside it.

questions.prompt: A four-part setting of G, C, D7, G at 72 beats per minute doubles the leading tone F sharp in the soprano and tenor, and moves soprano and alto from D and G to E and A, a perfect fifth apart, in similar motion. What are the two faults, what is a corrected soprano and alto pair, and how long is one 4/4 bar?
questions.answer: The tenor should take D or B so the leading tone sounds once, and soprano and alto should reach a third or sixth by contrary motion, for example D and G to B and G; one bar at 72 lasts 3.333 s
questions.distractor: Neither is a fault, because a leading tone may be doubled when it is in an inner voice and parallel fifths matter only between the outer voices
questions.correction: Doubling the leading tone gives two voices that must both resolve up to G, so the resolution arrives as a doubled tonic with no independence, which is why four-part practice doubles the root first and the fifth second while leaving the leading tone and the chordal seventh single. Parallel fifths are objectionable between any pair of voices, not only the outer pair, and the textbook reason is that they destroy the independence of the lines; a fifth to a fifth in similar motion does exactly that. At 72 beats per minute a beat is 0.833 s, so a 4/4 bar is 3.333 s and the progression lasts 13.333 s.

questions.prompt: Over a bar of C major the melody holds G from the previous bar into the downbeat and falls to F on beat 2. Later, on a weak beat, it leaps a fourth up to A and returns at once by step to G. A learner labels both notes passing tones. What are they, and what evidence decides?
questions.answer: The first is a 4-3 suspension: G is prepared on the same pitch, held as a dissonance over C and resolved down by step to F; the second is an escape tone, because it is approached by leap and left by step in the opposite direction
questions.distractor: Both are passing tones, because each note fills the gap between two chord tones and passing tones may be accented
questions.correction: A passing tone fills a third by step in one direction, so it must be approached and left by step, and it is normally unaccented; neither note here meets that description. A suspension requires three stages, preparation, suspension and resolution, and the textbook definition adds that it is approached by the same note and resolves down by step, with the interval pair named against the bass, so the held G over C falling to F is 4-3. The second note is approached by leap and left by step in the opposite direction, which is an escape tone; an appoggiatura would also be approached by leap but would resolve by step in the same direction as the leap.

questions.prompt: Against an eight-note cantus firmus in G major at 60 beats per minute, a learner writes a second line that starts a tenth below and moves in parallel tenths for six notes before leaping to the final G. Using first-species rules, what is wrong, and how long does the exercise last?
questions.answer: First species begins and ends on an octave or unison and approaches the close by contrary motion with 7 to 8 and 2 to 1; six parallel tenths break the limit of three consecutive imperfect consonances, and the leap into the final removes the required stepwise approach, so the exercise of eight whole notes lasts 32 s
questions.distractor: Nothing is wrong, because tenths are imperfect consonances and any number of them is permitted, and the final may be approached by leap as long as the interval is consonant
questions.correction: The textbook rules for first species allow imperfect consonances to be approached in any manner but forbid more than three consecutive thirds or sixths, and tenths are compound thirds, so six in a row is a fault. They also require the exercise to begin and end on an octave or unison, with the ending reached by contrary motion in which one part moves 7 to 8 and the other 2 to 1, adding a sharp to create the leading tone in a mode such as G Mixolydian. Permitted leaps are the third, fourth, fifth, ascending minor sixth and octave, so the final arrival must be prepared by step rather than by leap. Eight whole notes at 60 beats per minute occupy eight 4 s bars, which is 32.0 s.

questions.prompt: An eight-bar phrase in C major at 100 beats per minute moves one chord per bar: C, A minor, F, G, C, A minor, D7, G7. A producer who wants a bigger arrival doubles the chord rate in bars 5 to 8. What happens to the durations, and what would broaden the arrival instead?
questions.answer: One chord per bar gives each chord 2.4 s; doubling the rate cuts that to 1.2 s and makes the phrase accelerate into the cadence, while giving the dominant two bars at 4.8 s is what makes the arrival feel broad
questions.distractor: Harmonic rhythm is unaffected because the bar stays 2.4 s long whatever symbols are written above it, so only the chord labels change
questions.correction: Harmonic rhythm is defined as how long each chord lasts, so it is changed precisely by how many chords occupy a bar; at 100 beats per minute a beat is 0.6 s and a bar is 2.4 s, which means two chords per bar last 1.2 s each. Faster harmonic rhythm tends to push a phrase forward, which is useful in a middle section and counterproductive immediately before a cadence, where the ear needs the dominant to occupy time. The phrase model literature treats the arrival as the product of duration as well as function, so a dominant held for two bars, 4.8 s here, carries more weight than the same chord repeated at double speed.

questions.prompt: The same eight-bar progression is played three ways: a solo guitar melody with no accompaniment; guitar chords strummed in the same rhythm as the vocal; guitar chords plus an independent bass line while the vocal phrases across the bar lines. Name the three textures and say what changes between the second and third.
questions.answer: Monophony, then homophony in its homorhythmic form, then polyphony; the change is that the added bass becomes an independent line with its own rhythm rather than another voice moving at the same pace
questions.distractor: Monophony, then heterophony, then homophony, because the chords double the tune and the bass supplies the harmony underneath it
questions.correction: Heterophony requires several simultaneous variants of one melodic line, which is not what strummed chords are; they are harmony, and because they move at the same pace as the melody the texture is homophonic, specifically homorhythmic. Polyphony requires separate melodic lines and rhythms, which the independent bass and the across-the-bar vocal phrasing supply, so the third version is polyphonic even though only two lines are rhythmically free. The categories come from the standard texture chapter, which also warns that most music moves between them rather than sitting in one, so the useful answer names the texture bar by bar rather than for the whole piece.

units.title: Parts real players can play: transposition, ranges, spacing, tempo that breathes, and a three-part capstone

lessons.title: Transposing instruments: why the trumpet's written C sounds a B flat
lessons.explanation: A transposing instrument is one whose notation is not written at concert pitch, which is the pitch a non-transposing instrument such as the piano produces. The naming convention is the part learners find backwards: an instrument is named by the note that sounds when the player reads and fingers a written C. A written C on a B flat trumpet or clarinet sounds B flat, a major second below, so the instrument is in B flat; a written C on an E flat alto saxophone sounds E flat, a major sixth below; a written C on an F horn sounds F, a perfect fifth below; a written C on an A clarinet sounds A, a minor third below. The reason is construction rather than convention. A brass or woodwind instrument is a tube of a particular length, and that length fixes the scale it produces most naturally, so a B flat trumpet is built to sound a B flat scale from its open or fundamental position. Writing its music a major second higher than it sounds lets the player use one set of fingerings for the same written scale in every key, and it keeps the parts of a family of instruments in the same visual range. A second group transposes at the octave instead: the guitar and double bass sound an octave below their written notes, the piccolo an octave above, and the glockenspiel two octaves above. Scores come in two forms, a transposed score in which each part is written as the player reads it, and a score in C, also called a concert-pitch score, in which everything is written at sounding pitch.
lessons.example: Write a four-bar line in concert D major, running from D4 to B4, for three instruments at 88 beats per minute, where a bar is 2.727 s and the phrase lasts 10.909 s (computed). For the B flat trumpet, transpose up a major second: D4 becomes E4 and B4 becomes C sharp5, so the written part runs E4 to C sharp5, two semitones above the sounding pitch. The key follows the interval: D major has two sharps and a major second up adds two more, giving E major with four sharps. For the E flat alto saxophone, transpose up a major sixth: D4 becomes B4 and B4 becomes G sharp5, which is nine semitones up, and D major with two sharps becomes B major with five. For the horn in F, transpose up a perfect fifth: D4 becomes A4 and B4 becomes F sharp5, seven semitones up, and D major becomes A major with three sharps. Check each by reversing the interval: E4 down a major second is D4, B4 down a major sixth is D4, A4 down a perfect fifth is D4, so all three written parts sound the same concert line. Notice that the written ranges differ by more than an octave in total while the sounding pitch does not move at all, which is the point of the convention: each player sees a part in a comfortable reading range for their instrument.
lessons.question: A concert-pitch part in F major, from F4 to D5, is handed to a B flat clarinettist, who plays it as written. What does the audience hear, and what should the part have been?
lessons.answer: The audience hears E flat major, a major second below F, running from E flat4 to C5; the part should have been written a major second higher in G major, from G4 to E5, with one sharp instead of one flat
lessons.distractor: The audience hears F major as written and only the tone colour changes, because a B flat clarinet can play any key and the player compensates automatically
lessons.correction: The player does not compensate, because reading a part means fingering what is printed and trusting that the notation has already been transposed; a written F on a B flat clarinet sounds E flat, so the whole part arrives a major second low and every chord built on it is wrong by the same interval. The correction is arithmetic plus notation: transpose up a major second, which moves F to G and D to E, and move the key signature with it, so F major with one flat becomes G major with one sharp. Clarinettists can play in F major, and that is not the issue; the issue is that the part on the stand must be written in the key that produces concert F when fingered. This is the single most common delivery error in arranging for winds, and it is inaudible to the arranger until the first rehearsal.

depth.definitions: Concert pitch is sounding pitch, the pitch a piano or a non-transposing instrument produces. Written pitch is what appears on the page. The transposition interval is named by the sounding note of a written C, and the direction is always given from written to sounding. A B flat instrument sounds a major second below written pitch, an E flat instrument a major sixth below, an F instrument a perfect fifth below, an A instrument a minor third below. Octave-transposing instruments keep the letter name and shift the register: guitar and double bass sound an octave below, piccolo an octave above, glockenspiel two octaves above. A transposed score writes each part as the player reads it; a score in C writes everything at sounding pitch. MIDI note numbers count semitones from a fixed reference, so transposition in a sequencer is adding or subtracting a constant. Prerequisites: key signatures from lesson 33, interval arithmetic from lesson 32, the circle of fifths from lesson 42, and the movable shapes and capo of lesson 54, which solve the same problem on the guitar by changing shape rather than by changing notation.
depth.mechanism: Instrument length sets the natural scale, and notation is bent to fit the instrument rather than the other way round. A tube that sounds a B flat fundamental produces its simplest scale from that pitch, and its player learns one fingering pattern that reads as a C scale on the page and sounds as a B flat scale. Transposing the part keeps that pattern valid in every key, so a player can move between a B flat trumpet, a C trumpet and an E flat trumpet without relearning fingerings, and the whole family reads in similar registers. The cost is that every part in a score has to be converted, which is why scores in C exist for study and conducting while parts are transposed. Octave transposition has a different motive: the guitar's written range covers the treble staff so that its music looks like other treble-clef music, and the sounding octave below is simply a convention attached to the instrument. Both kinds are silent in performance, since the player reads and the instrument speaks.
depth.secondExample: Octave transposition causes errors that survive a whole session because nothing looks wrong on the page. Copy a piano right-hand melody that sits between C4 and C5 onto a guitar staff without adjustment, and a guitarist reading it will sound between C3 and C4, an octave below the piano, which is often inaudible in isolation and obvious the moment the two play together. The double bass has the same relationship to the bass staff, and the piccolo the opposite one, sounding an octave above. In a sequencer the question becomes a convention rather than a notation rule: MIDI note number 60 is middle C in the labelling most DAWs use, though some manufacturers print it as C3, so a guitar library may be mapped to sound an octave below the note numbers you enter. The diagnostic is to play a single written C4 on each instrument, check the sounding pitch against a piano or a tuner, and write the offset on the part: plus two for the trumpet, plus nine for the alto sax, minus twelve for the guitar.
depth.mistake: The first error is transposing in the wrong direction, which is easy because the instrument name states its sounding pitch and not the direction of the notation. The rule to memorise is that the written part is always in the opposite direction from the sounding note: an instrument that sounds lower is written higher. The second is transposing the notes and forgetting the key signature, which leaves a part that is correct in pitch and wrong in the accidentals it applies. The third is assuming the guitar reads at concert pitch, which produces parts an octave high in the mix. The fourth is handing a concert-pitch score to a transposing player, which is the error in this lesson's question and the one that wastes the most rehearsal time. A ten-second diagnostic before any session: name the written key, name the sounding key, and check the interval arithmetic in semitones rather than by eye.
depth.application: Task in one session of 25 minutes at a desk, plus ten minutes with an instrument or a piano. Take an eight-bar melody in a key you know and produce three written versions: for B flat trumpet, for E flat alto saxophone and for F horn. Write the sounding key first, then the written key, then the transposition in semitones, then the written range. Finally play the concert melody on a keyboard and sing or play each written version down the transposition interval to confirm it matches. Model answer for a concert line in B flat major from F4 to D5: trumpet written C major from G4 to E5, up two semitones; alto sax written G major from D5 to B5, up nine semitones; horn written F major from C5 to A5, up seven semitones. Self-review rubric: one point for the correct direction on all three, one for a key signature that matches the transposition, one for the written range stated in scientific pitch notation, one for a sung or played check that the sounding result matches. Warm up before playing, keep the instrument at a comfortable level, and stop if your voice or hands feel strained.
depth.summary: A transposing instrument is named by the pitch that sounds when a written C is played, so its part is written in the opposite direction from its sounding pitch. Trumpet and clarinet in B flat are written a major second higher, alto saxophone in E flat a major sixth higher, horn in F a perfect fifth higher, and guitar and double bass an octave higher than they sound. Transpose the notes, the key signature and the range together, and check the result by reversing the interval.

lessons.title: Ranges and tessitura: writing parts a player can actually play and sing
lessons.explanation: A range is the set of pitches an instrument or voice can produce; a tessitura is the part of that range where the music actually sits, and the second matters more than the first in practice. Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom is explicit that its four-part ranges are deliberately narrower than what real singers can reach, and that they are based on the ranges found in Bach's 371 chorales, which is a useful standard because those parts were written to be sung by ordinary singers in ordinary churches. In that standard the soprano runs C4 to A5, the alto G3 to E5, the tenor C3 to A4 and the bass E2 to E4. Convert those to semitone spans and three of them are identical: soprano, alto and tenor each cover 21 semitones, while the bass covers 24. A professional orchestral player will have a wider compass than this, and an amateur or a beginner a narrower one, so the working assumption should be the chorale range unless you know the player. Two further distinctions are needed. An extreme is a note that is reachable but expensive, reliable once or twice in a piece and unsafe as a destination; a comfortable note can be sustained for bars without fatigue. And every instrument has a register break, the passaggio in a voice or the point where a brass player changes partials, where control is least secure and intonation most at risk.
lessons.example: Check a sixteen-bar chorale-style passage at 66 beats per minute, where a beat is 0.909 s, a bar is 3.636 s and the passage lasts 58.182 s (computed), against the four ranges. The soprano sits between E4 and D5, which is inside C4 to A5 with seven semitones of headroom at the top, so it is comfortable. The alto sits between A3 and C5, inside G3 to E5. The tenor is written on G4 for twelve consecutive bars, and although G4 is inside C3 to A4, it is only two semitones below the ceiling, so the passage asks for 43.636 s of near-extreme singing, which is a tessitura fault even though every individual note is legal. The bass is written on F4, which is above E4 and therefore outside the range altogether, and the fix cannot be a small adjustment; the line has to be dropped an octave to F3 or the note has to move to another voice. Now measure each part's span as a check on the arrangement: the soprano line covers ten semitones from E4 to D5, the alto fifteen from A3 to C5, and the tenor and the corrected bass each stay on a single pitch. The alto's fifteen semitones are 71.4 per cent of its 21-semitone compass, which is wide but centred, so it is a line with a range rather than a line at a limit. The tenor's problem is duration and not span, which is why counting semitones alone would have missed it.
lessons.question: A guitarist writes a melody that sits between the twelfth and fifteenth frets for a sixteen-bar section, then gives the same part to a singer whose comfortable range is C3 to C4. What are the two problems, and what is the practical fix?
lessons.answer: The guitar part is in a thin, high position where the short vibrating length gives little body, and the melody lies more than an octave above the singer's comfortable top; the fix is to transpose the whole section down to the singer's key and re-voice the guitar in a lower position rather than to ask either player to stretch
lessons.distractor: Neither is a problem, because both parts are inside their written ranges and a player who can reach a note can sustain it for a section
lessons.correction: Reachability and tessitura are different questions: a note at the fifteenth fret is inside the guitar's range and still sounds thin because the vibrating length is short and the string is stiff relative to its length, so the fundamental is weak. For the singer, C4 is the top of the comfortable range, which means a melody that sits above it is not merely difficult but outside the working compass, and no amount of rehearsal will make sixteen bars there reliable. The arrangement fix is a transposition, chosen by finding the key where the melody sits in the middle of the singer's range, and then re-voicing the guitar part in a lower position so that the accompaniment keeps body. This is what a capo does in reverse: it changes the sounding key without changing the shapes, which is why lesson 54 treated it as a transposition tool.

depth.definitions: Range is the compass of pitches an instrument or voice can produce. Tessitura is the portion of that range a piece actually occupies, weighted by duration. A working or comfortable range is the part available for sustained use; an extreme is reachable but costly. A register break or passaggio is the transition between vocal registers or brass partials where control is weakest. Written range is what appears on the page and sounding range is what is heard, which differ for the octave-transposing instruments of lesson 86. Doubling at the octave extends a line without extending its range. Prerequisites: scientific pitch notation from lesson 33 and the notation section of lesson 86, chord spacing from lesson 81, inversions from lesson 57, capo transposition from lesson 54, and the vocal coordination work of lesson 58, which is where the difference between a comfortable and a strained note first becomes audible.
depth.mechanism: Range is set by physical limits: vocal fold length and tension, string length and tension, the length of a tube and the partials it will support, and the mechanics of a key or a slide. Tessitura is set by fatigue, and fatigue accumulates with time rather than with pitch, which is why twelve bars on the second-highest note of a range is harder than one bar on the highest. For voices, the passaggio is where the balance between the muscle that thins the folds and the muscle that thickens them changes over, and notes near it are the least stable in tuning and tone. For strings, a shorter vibrating length gives a brighter, thinner sound with less fundamental, which is why the same pitch played high on a low string sounds different from the open string above it. For brass, high notes require faster lip vibration and more support, so endurance is consumed far faster in the upper register. None of these limits appear in a chord symbol, which is why a range check has to be a separate step.
depth.secondExample: The same pitch can be comfortable or marginal depending on where it is played, and the guitar makes this visible. E5 can be played on the open first string, at the fifth fret of the second string, the ninth fret of the third string or the fourteenth fret of the fourth string; the pitch is identical and the tone is not, because the vibrating lengths differ by a factor of more than two and the shorter string produces a weaker fundamental and a faster decay. A melody that stays above the twelfth fret for a whole section therefore has a tessitura problem even though every note is inside the instrument's range, and the arranger's fix is to move it to a lower position or to a different key rather than to ask for more force. For a singer the same arithmetic applies to key choice: if a melody sits between C4 and A4 and the singer's comfortable range is A3 to G4, transposing down a minor third puts the melody between A3 and F sharp4, inside the range and without changing its shape, which is the decision a musical director makes in the first rehearsal rather than the tenth.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is judging range by staff position, so a bass part on F4 looks unremarkable because it sits inside the bass clef and is in fact above the chorale ceiling for the voice. The diagnostic is to convert every part to scientific pitch notation and compare it with the range, not with the staff. A second error is writing for the extremes because a professional could manage them, which produces parts that are playable once and unreliable in a run of performances. A third is ignoring duration: a page of high notes for a tenor is a different proposition from one high note in sixteen bars, and the check has to count bars as well as semitones. A fourth is assuming that a wide range implies a wide comfortable range, which confuses what an instrument can do on a good day with what a part can ask for every night.
depth.application: Task in one session of 25 minutes with a score or a lead sheet and an instrument. Take a piece you play or sing and write the lowest and highest note of each part in scientific pitch notation, then the same for the section that lasts longest at one pitch. Compare each part with the chorale ranges given in this lesson and mark every note within two semitones of a limit. For each mark, decide whether it is a destination, which may be an extreme, or a sustained passage, which may not. Then rewrite one part so that its tessitura sits in the middle third of its range, and play or sing the result. Model answer for the sixteen-bar example: soprano E4 to D5, comfortable; alto A3 to C5, comfortable; tenor G4 for twelve bars, a tessitura fault at 43.636 s near the ceiling; bass F4, out of range and to be moved to F3; corrected spans of ten and fifteen semitones with the tenor and bass each on a single pitch. Self-review rubric: one point for scientific pitch notation used consistently, one for a duration counted in seconds, one for a distinction between destination and sustained passage, one for a rewrite that improves tessitura without changing the harmony. Warm up before singing or playing, keep the effort moderate, and stop at the first sign of strain rather than pushing for the top note.
depth.summary: Range tells you which notes exist for an instrument; tessitura tells you which notes the music asks for and for how long. The chorale standard gives soprano C4 to A5, alto G3 to E5, tenor C3 to A4 and bass E2 to E4, and the working rule is to keep sustained writing in the middle of that compass and to spend extremes only on destinations. Check every part in scientific pitch notation, count duration as well as pitch, and transpose or revoice rather than asking a player to stretch.
