lessons.title: Spacing and doubling: why the same chord thins out in the low register
lessons.explanation: Two arrangements can contain exactly the same chord tones and sound completely different, and the difference is spacing and doubling. Spacing is described as close or open depending on whether the upper voices sit within an octave or are spread across two. The rule that governs it is stated plainly in the four-part chapter: keep soprano to alto and alto to tenor within an octave of each other, but allow the bass to sit further below the tenor. The justification given there is the overtone series, in which the intervals between adjacent partials are wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, and orchestration guidance repeats the shape: use wide gaps in the bass register, denser packing in the middle, and wider spacing again at the very top. Doubling is the second decision. In a triad the doubling order is root, then fifth, then third, and orchestration texts add a specific warning against over-doubling the third, because the third is what defines the mode and too many statements of it tilt the chord towards the mediant. A seventh chord normally states all four tones once. Put the two decisions together and you can predict, before playing a note, whether a chord will sound solid, thin or muddy.
lessons.example: Play a C major triad three ways on a piano and compare the numbers. Version one is close position at the bottom of the instrument: C2, E2, G2. Version two is open: C2, G2, C3, E3. Version three is spread across three octaves: C2, C3, G3, E4. The pitch classes are identical in all three. Now look at the intervals in hertz rather than in semitones. C2 is 65.41 Hz and E2 is 82.41 Hz, so the major third between them is 17.00 Hz wide, while the fifth from C2 to G2 is 32.59 Hz and the octave from C2 to C3 is 65.41 Hz. The ear's frequency filters at that pitch are on the order of 100 Hz wide, so in version one all three fundamentals and several of their lower partials fall inside a single filter and the chord is heard as one rough, thick event rather than as three pitches. Version two keeps one wide gap at the bottom, from C2 up to G2, then closes the upper voices to a fourth and a third, so the fundamentals separate while the upper voices still blend. Version three is so open that the chord stops sounding like a chord and starts sounding like an arpeggio played simultaneously. The textbook account of why some voicings ring and others do not is exactly this: the spacing of the lower partials follows the same widening as the overtone series.
lessons.question: An arranger writes a C major chord for a string section as C2, E2, G2, C3 and then adds a second cello on E3 to strengthen the third. What will the section sound like, and what should change?
lessons.answer: Thick and mode-heavy, because the bass has a close major third of 17.00 Hz between C2 and E2 and the third is doubled twice; open the bottom to C2 and G2, keep the upper voices within an octave, and double the root rather than the third
lessons.distractor: Fuller and clearer, because adding a second statement of the third strengthens the major quality and close spacing at the bottom keeps the section together
lessons.correction: The third does define the major quality, and that is precisely why doubling it weights the chord towards E and away from C: with C stated twice and E stated twice, the sonority has no clear root and can be heard as a first-inversion chord. The spacing compounds the problem, since C2 and E2 are only 17.00 Hz apart and their partials overlap inside one critical band, producing roughness rather than definition. Orchestration guidance is to include all the important harmonic pitches, avoid over-doubling the third, keep larger gaps in the bass and denser packing in the middle. The repair is to open the low interval, for example C2 and G2, place C3 and E3 above, and give the extra cello the root or the fifth, which adds weight without changing the balance of the chord.

depth.definitions: Spacing is the distance between adjacent voices; close position keeps the upper three within an octave, open position spreads them further. A gap is the interval between two adjacent voices, and an overlap is a voice moving beyond the previous pitch of its neighbour. Doubling gives a chord tone to more than one voice; omission leaves one out. A low interval limit is the practical rule that close intervals in the bass sound muddy regardless of how correct they are on paper. A critical band is the range of frequencies the ear's filters treat as one event, roughly 100 Hz wide at low frequencies and proportionally wider higher up. Root position, inversion and drop voicings describe which chord tone is in the bass and how the upper parts are distributed. Prerequisites: triad construction from lesson 34, inversion and bass position from lesson 57, the spacing and doubling rules of lesson 81, and the masking discussion of lesson 39, which is the mixing version of the same acoustic problem.
depth.mechanism: The ear analyses pitch through filters whose bandwidth is roughly constant in hertz at low frequencies, which means that a fixed musical interval occupies a smaller and smaller fraction of a filter as you go down. At C2 a major third is 17 Hz, well inside one filter, so the two fundamentals and their lower partials are not resolved separately; the result is beating and roughness rather than two clear pitches. At C5 the same major third is about 136 Hz, wider than a filter, so the two notes separate. That is why the overtone series and the spacing rule agree: nature puts wide intervals at the bottom of a spectrum, and voicings that imitate that shape sound clear. Doubling works the other way, because every added statement of a pitch adds energy at its fundamental and its partials, so doubling the root reinforces the pitch that identifies the chord while doubling the third competes with it. None of this is style-dependent, which is why the same advice appears in chorale writing, orchestration manuals and mixing guides.
depth.secondExample: The guitar makes the same point with two voicings of one chord. An open C major shape sounds C3, E3, G3, C4 and E4, with the third doubled and all five notes inside an octave and a half, which is why it sounds full in a mix where the bass is playing C2: the low interval is supplied by another instrument and the guitar stays in its own register. Play the same chord as a barre shape at the eighth fret, and the sounding pitches move to C4 upwards, so the chord now sits above the bass and above the vocal, and it will sound thin and separated unless something else covers the middle. A jazz drop-2 voicing solves a different version of the problem by removing the root from the upper structure and leaving it to the bass, which keeps the middle register clear for a vocal. In every case the question is the same: which pitch classes, in which octaves, with which gaps, and what is doubling what.
depth.mistake: The usual error is to treat open spacing as a licence to spread every voice, which produces a chord with a hole in the middle that sounds hollow and cannot be balanced. The diagnostic is to measure the three gaps separately: bass to tenor, tenor to alto, alto to soprano. A second error is doubling the third because it is the note that makes the chord major, which unbalances the sonority and can make a root-position chord sound inverted. A third is judging spacing by eye on a score, where a third at the bottom of the bass staff looks identical to a third at the top of the treble staff; the check is to convert the interval to hertz before deciding. A fourth is adding octave doublings to compensate for a muddy voicing, which adds level without adding clarity.
depth.application: Task in one session of 25 minutes with a piano, a guitar or a DAW and a frequency reference such as a tuner or a piano roll. Play or program a C major triad in the three voicings described in the example and, for each, write the interval in semitones and in hertz between adjacent voices. Then make a fourth version that doubles the third and describe what changed in one sentence. Finally choose the voicing that would work under a bass guitar playing C2 and above a vocal singing E4, and justify it with the gap measurements. Model answer for the three versions: C2 E2 G2 has gaps of 4 and 3 semitones, 17.00 Hz and 15.59 Hz, and is muddy; C2 G2 C3 E3 has gaps of 7, 5 and 4 semitones and separates the low end; C2 C3 G3 E4 has gaps of 12, 7 and 9 semitones and sounds like a broken chord. Self-review rubric: one point for hertz converted correctly, one for identifying the low gap as the problem, one for a doubling decision justified by the root, one for a voicing chosen to fit the register of the other parts. Keep the playback level moderate, take breaks, and stop if your ears feel fatigued by repeated low chords.
depth.summary: Spacing controls clarity and doubling controls weight, and both can be predicted from frequency rather than guessed from taste. Keep the upper voices close, open the bass, double the root before the fifth and the fifth before the third, and remember that the same interval is narrow in hertz at the bottom of the range and wide at the top. A voicing that respects the overtone series will sit in a mix without equalisation.

lessons.title: Tempo that breathes: written tempo, rubato and the tempo map
lessons.explanation: Tempo is the rate of the beat, and it is the one parameter that changes the duration of everything else without changing a single note value. Open Music Theory treats a tempo indication as one of the elements of notation alongside dynamics and articulation, and the practical consequence is that a page can specify a speed, slow it down and speed it up again, and expect three different elapsed times from the same bar count. Four terms cover most of what a learner needs. A metronome mark fixes beats per minute and is the only unambiguous tempo instruction. An Italian term such as allegro or adagio gives a range rather than a number and depends on the era and the piece. A ritardando or accelerando is a gradual change written over several beats, not a switch at the end. Rubato is a localised pushing and pulling of the tempo, usually with the melody taking time and the accompaniment keeping it, and it is a relationship between parts rather than a licence to ignore the pulse. In a DAW all of this lives in a tempo map or tempo track: a list of tempo values placed at bar and beat positions, which re-times note data automatically and forces recorded audio to be warped or re-performed. Lesson 52 dealt with practising to a click; this lesson is about the opposite skill, playing and notating time that moves on purpose.
lessons.example: Take a four-bar phrase at 96 beats per minute with a ritardando written over the final bar, down to 72. At a steady 96 a beat is 0.625 s and a 4/4 bar is 2.5 s, so four bars last 10.0 s (computed). Now calculate the final bar properly, because a ritardando is a continuous change rather than a slower tempo applied at the bar line: if the tempo falls evenly from 96 to 72 across the four beats, the bar takes 2.877 s, its average tempo is 240 divided by 2.877, which is 83.4 beats per minute, and the phrase grows to 10.377 s. That is an addition of 0.377 s, about 3.8 per cent, which is roughly the difference a listener hears as leaning into the close rather than as a mistake. Compare a fermata on the final chord, which adds an unmeasured pause, and a written bar of 72 beats per minute, which would take 3.333 s and add 0.833 s, more than twice as much. The distinction matters in a DAW: a tempo map can represent the gradual change exactly, while a single project tempo of 96 leaves the phrase 0.377 s short and the audio drifting ahead of the score by the end of four bars.
lessons.question: A pianist records a four-bar introduction without a click, then imports the audio into a project set to 96 beats per minute and finds the last chord arrives before the grid. What has happened, and what are the two honest solutions?
lessons.answer: The performance contains a ritardando that a single project tempo cannot represent, so the audio finishes about 0.377 s early against a steady grid; either build a tempo map that follows the take, or re-perform it to a click and keep 96 fixed
lessons.distractor: The recording is late because the pianist rushed, and the only solution is to quantise the audio to the grid so that every chord lands on a beat
lessons.correction: The arithmetic identifies the cause before any repair is attempted: a four-bar phrase at 96 lasts 10.0 s, and the same phrase with the last bar slowing to 72 lasts 10.377 s, so a take that breathes will always end ahead of a fixed grid rather than behind it. Quantising audio to a steady grid removes the ritardando that was the point of the performance, replacing expression with alignment. The two honest options are to let the performance define the time, which means mapping the tempo bar by bar and beat by beat so that the grid follows the take, or to fix the time and re-perform the phrase against a click at 96, accepting a straighter ending. Which one to choose depends on whether the take or the grid is the reference, and that decision should be made before any editing begins.

depth.definitions: Tempo is the rate of the beat, measured in beats per minute when it is exact. A metronome mark gives a number and a note value, such as a quarter note at 96. A tempo indication is a word or phrase, from grave to prestissimo, that specifies a character as well as a speed. Ritardando and rallentando slow gradually; accelerando speeds up gradually; a fermata holds a note beyond its written value. Rubato is a temporary departure from strict tempo, usually within a phrase and usually restored by its end. Tempo giusto means strict tempo. A tempo map or tempo track stores tempo values at bar and beat positions. Warping stretches recorded audio to fit a tempo without changing its pitch, at the cost of artefacts. Prerequisites: pulse and metre from lessons 51 and 53, metronome practice from lesson 52, count-ins from lesson 63, the tempo ladder of lesson 65, and the note-data and audio distinction of lesson 78.
depth.mechanism: Listeners infer tempo from the intervals between onsets, and they update that inference continuously, which is why a gradual change is heard as expression while an abrupt one is heard as an edit. A slowdown distributed across four beats is heard as a bend, because each inter-onset interval grows by only a few per cent, while the same total applied at the bar line is heard as a lurch, because one interval grows by a quarter. Scale matters as well: a change of five to ten per cent reads as expressive shading, and a quarter of the tempo confined to one beat reads as an error. Rubato adds a second layer, because when the melody and the accompaniment disagree about time, the listener follows the melody and treats the accompaniment as the reference, and that relationship is what makes the device work without the pulse being lost. In a sequencer, tempo is applied to the timeline rather than to the notes, so a tempo change re-times everything that is not audio.
depth.secondExample: Consider the same four bars in a session where the drums were programmed to a grid and the vocal was sung afterwards. The drums are note data or audio locked to 96 beats per minute, so setting a tempo map that slows the last bar will pull the drum events with the grid, which produces the intended ritardando automatically. The vocal, if it was recorded against the click, is audio and will not follow; it has to be warped with markers placed on its syllables, or the phrase has to be sung again over the mapped tempo. This is the practical reason to decide the order of work before recording: fix the tempo map first and record everything against it, and no warping is needed; record freely and map afterwards, and every audio track needs markers. The musical version of the same decision appears in a string quartet, where the players breathe the tempo together because they are watching each other rather than a click, and the written score shows a ritardando that the ensemble realises in a way no metronome mark can specify.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is placing the whole slowdown on the last beat, which produces a lurch rather than a lean; the diagnostic is to write the intended tempo at each beat of the final bar and check that the differences are small and even. A second error is treating rubato as permission to abandon the pulse, which loses the ensemble and makes the return impossible to place. A third is notating a tempo change as a note value change, writing longer notes where the music should merely slow, which alters the metre instead of the speed. A fourth, specific to production, is setting a single project tempo for a performance that moves and then blaming the performer for sounding early, when the map is the missing element. The check is always the same: compute the duration under both readings and compare it with what the take actually lasts.
depth.application: Task in one session of 30 minutes with an instrument and a metronome or a DAW. Set 96 beats per minute and play a four-bar phrase with a written ritardando in the last bar, then record it twice: once at a fixed 96 and once with the slowdown. Measure both durations against the computed values of 10.0 s and 10.377 s, and note the difference in milliseconds per beat across the final bar. Then build a tempo map in the DAW with four tempo values, 96, 96, 96 and a final bar that steps down in even increments to 72, and check that the grid lands where the performance did. Model answer: steady version 10.0 s, breathing version 10.377 s, final bar 2.877 s at an average of 83.4 beats per minute, difference 0.377 s or 377 ms spread across four beats, which is about 94 ms per beat on average. Self-review rubric: one point for the arithmetic, one for a ritardando spread across the bar rather than the last beat, one for a tempo map that matches the take, one written sentence on whether the grid or the take was treated as the reference. Keep monitoring levels moderate, warm up before playing, and stop if a hand or wrist aches during repeated takes.
depth.summary: Tempo is applied to time rather than to notes, so a ritardando changes duration without changing notation: four bars at 96 last 10.0 s, and the same four bars with the last one slowing to 72 last 10.377 s. Write gradual changes across a bar, keep rubato inside the pulse, and in a DAW decide whether the grid or the take is the reference before recording, because note data follows a tempo map and audio has to be warped or re-performed.

lessons.title: Capstone: score sixteen bars for three parts, then prove it in the session
lessons.explanation: This lesson assembles the unit into one deliverable: sixteen bars, three parts, a written score and a rendered file, with every decision justified by a rule learned since lesson 81. The order of work matters more than the talent applied to any single step. First fix the harmony and its rhythm, because harmonic rhythm decides how much time every other decision has. Then write the principal melody, check it against the chord tones and label whatever non-chord tones you used. Then write the second line as counterpoint rather than as a doubling, checking consonance on strong beats and motion between them. Then assign parts to instruments: choose the instrument for each line, transpose the written parts, check every part against its range and tessitura, and voice the chords so that the lower register is open and the upper register is close. Finally set the time: write the tempo, place the ritardando where it belongs, compute the total duration, and confirm that every part carries the same instruction. A score that satisfies all of that can be played by three strangers in one rehearsal, which is the only test of an arrangement that matters.
lessons.example: Take the plan for a sixteen-bar piece at 92 beats per minute, where a beat is 0.652 s and a bar is 2.609 s, for B flat clarinet, guitar and bass guitar in concert D major (computed). Harmonic rhythm: two chords per bar for bars one to eight, at 1.304 s each; one chord per bar for bars nine to fourteen, at 2.609 s; and one chord held across bars fifteen and sixteen, at 5.217 s, which is the broadening before the close. Melody: concert A4 to D5, which for the clarinet becomes written B4 to E5 in E major with four sharps, a major second above the sounding line and inside the instrument's working range. Guitar: written in the treble clef an octave above its sound, so the part is notated between D4 and D5 and sounds between D3 and D4, which leaves the middle register to the clarinet. Bass guitar: written D3 to D4, sounding D2 to D3, roots and fifths only, with the fifth omitted when the guitar already has it. Voice leading: the guitar plays three-note shapes in the upper register, the bass takes roots, and the clarinet line is checked against both for parallel fifths, which is possible to do by eye once the parts are written in concert pitch. Timing: sixteen bars at 92 last 41.739 s, and the final bar slowing to 69 takes 3.002 s instead of 2.609 s, so the piece lasts 42.132 s and every part must show the ritardando.
lessons.question: A three-part arrangement is finished in a score at concert pitch and sent to a clarinettist in B flat, a guitarist and a bassist. The clarinettist plays in the wrong key, the guitar sounds an octave below the piano reduction, and the final ritardando is heard only in the guitar. What are the three faults and what does each fix?
lessons.answer: The score must be transposed per part rather than delivered in C, so the clarinet part is written a major second higher in the written key, the guitar and bass parts are marked as sounding an octave below their written notes, and the ritardando must appear in all three parts and in the tempo map
lessons.distractor: The players should transpose at sight, the guitar should be restrung or capoed to match the piano, and the ritardando should be conducted rather than written, since expression belongs to the performers
lessons.correction: Transposition is the arranger's job because the notation is part of the deliverable: a clarinettist reading a concert-pitch part produces a major second below the intended key, which is not a matter of skill. The octave relationship is a property of the instrument and cannot be fixed by a capo, since a capo changes the sounding key rather than the octave convention; the part is written an octave above its sound and that has to be stated on the page. The ritardando is a tempo instruction, and a tempo instruction that appears in one part only will be played by one player only, so it belongs in every part and in the tempo map of the session. All three faults share a cause: the arrangement was checked as music and not as a set of parts that other people have to read.

depth.definitions: A score presents all parts together; a part is the extract one player reads. A concert-pitch score, or score in C, writes everything at sounding pitch, while a transposed score writes each part as the player reads it. A cue is a short quotation of another part printed in a rest so the player can find their entry. A tempo map is the list of tempo values for the session. A delivery note states the tempo, the duration, the instrumentation, the transpositions and any instruction that is not visible on the page. Doubling means two instruments on one line; divisi means splitting a section. Prerequisites: every lesson in this unit, and behind them voice leading from lesson 81, non-chord tones from lesson 82, counterpoint from lesson 83, harmonic rhythm from lesson 84, texture from lesson 85, transposition from lesson 86, ranges from lesson 87, spacing from lesson 88 and tempo from lesson 89, with the production workflow of lessons 78 and 80 for the rendered file.
depth.mechanism: The capstone works because each rule removes a class of failure that cannot be heard until the parts are played by other people. Voice leading removes collisions that only appear when two players sustain a chord. Non-chord tone labels make the melody's dissonances intentional, so a player knows which notes to lean on. Counterpoint keeps the second line from being a doubling, which is what makes three players sound like three parts. Harmonic rhythm gives the phrase a shape that survives an imperfect performance. Range and tessitura checks prevent the failure that cannot be fixed in rehearsal, a part that is simply too high for the player in front of you. Transposition prevents the failure that cannot be fixed at all without rewriting. Spacing prevents the low-register mud that no mixer can remove. And the tempo map keeps the parts together when the music slows. Every one of these is cheaper to fix on paper than in a room.
depth.secondExample: Change one instrument and the arithmetic changes while the music does not. Replace the clarinet with an alto saxophone in E flat and the same concert line from A4 to D5 must be written a major sixth higher, from F sharp5 to B5, in B major with five sharps instead of E major with four; the sounding result is identical and the player's reading range is different, which may push the top of the line against the instrument's comfortable register. Replace the guitar with a piano and the octave convention disappears, but the spacing problem arrives, since the piano will double the bass guitar's register unless the left hand is kept above it. Neither substitution is better; each changes which rules do the work. The test of the arrangement is therefore not whether it sounds right on the instruments you happened to choose, but whether the parts still satisfy the rules after a substitution, which is what a score in C plus written parts allows you to check.
depth.mistake: The characteristic error at this stage is delivering a concert-pitch score and calling it an arrangement, which shifts the transposition onto the players and fails at the first rehearsal. The second is checking the music without checking the parts: ranges, page turns, cues and the placement of the ritardando are part of the deliverable. The third is mistaking a rendered file for a finished piece, when the file proves the sound and the parts prove the arrangement. The fourth is leaving the tempo instruction to a conductor who will not be there, which is how a ritardando becomes a rallentando in one part and nothing in another. The diagnostic before sending anything is a checklist read aloud against the score: every part transposed, every part inside its range, every sustained note justified, every tempo instruction in every part, and a duration computed rather than estimated.
depth.application: The task is the capstone itself, planned across three sessions of about 40 minutes and finished in one. Session one, on paper: choose sixteen bars, fix the harmonic rhythm in three phases as in the example, write the melody, and label every non-chord tone. Session two: write the second line as counterpoint, check the strong-beat intervals, and voice the chords with the bass open and the upper parts close. Session three: assign the instruments, transpose each part, check ranges and tessitura, add the ritardando to every part, and compute the total duration. Then render a file and write a delivery note that states tempo, duration, instrumentation, transpositions and the one decision you are least sure about. Model delivery note for the example: sixteen bars in concert D major at 92 beats per minute, 42.132 s including a final-bar ritardando to 69, for B flat clarinet (written E major), guitar (sounding an octave below written) and bass guitar (sounding an octave below written), with the clarinet line from written B4 to E5 and the guitar confined to the upper register. Self-review rubric: one point for harmonic rhythm stated in seconds, one for a countermelody that is not a doubling, one for correct transposition and range checks, one for a tempo instruction in every part, one for a delivery note that names an uncertainty honestly. Warm up before playing, keep the session under an hour with a break, and stop if a hand, wrist or voice shows strain.
depth.summary: An arrangement is finished when three strangers could play it from the parts you sent. Fix harmony and harmonic rhythm, write and label the melody, write the second line as counterpoint, assign and transpose the parts, check ranges and spacing, place the tempo instructions everywhere they are needed, compute the duration, and state the whole thing in a delivery note. The rules from lessons 81 to 89 are not separate topics; they are the checklist that makes the deliverable playable.

questions.prompt: A four-bar line in concert D major, running from D4 to B4, is to be written for B flat trumpet and for E flat alto saxophone. In what written key and range does each part appear, and which part carries more sharps?
questions.answer: The trumpet part is written in E major, four sharps, from E4 to C sharp5, sounding a major second lower; the alto sax part is written in B major, five sharps, from B4 to G sharp5, sounding a major sixth lower, so the saxophone part has one more sharp
questions.distractor: Both parts are written in D major with two sharps, because a transposing instrument reads concert pitch and the player adjusts the fingering to match
questions.correction: Transposing instruments are notated at a transposed pitch, and the interval is named by what a written C produces: a written C on a B flat instrument sounds B flat, a major second lower, and a written C on an E flat alto saxophone sounds E flat, a major sixth lower. To sound concert D the trumpet part is therefore written up a major second, in E major, and the saxophone part up a major sixth, in B major, since writing it down would put it below the instrument's range and produce the wrong sounding key. Adding an interval to a key signature adds sharps in the same proportion, so D major with two sharps becomes E major with four and B major with five, and the sounding range falls to B3 to G4 on the trumpet and F3 to D4 on the saxophone.

questions.prompt: A bass part is written on F4 for sixteen bars at 60 beats per minute in a chorale-style arrangement. Using ranges derived from Bach's chorales, what is the problem, how long does the passage last, and what are two fixes that keep the harmony?
questions.answer: The bass range tops out near E4, so F4 sits above it for 64 s; move the line to F3 an octave lower, or give the F to the tenor and let the bass take the root underneath
questions.distractor: There is no problem, because F4 sits inside the bass staff, and sixteen bars at 60 beats per minute last 16 s
questions.correction: Staff position is not range: the chorale-based ranges place the bass from E2 to E4, so F4 is above the top of the working range and sixteen bars of it is a tessitura problem rather than a single high note. At 60 beats per minute a beat is 1 s, so a 4/4 bar is 4 s and sixteen bars are 64 s, not 16 s, which is long enough for the strain to be audible. Dropping the line an octave preserves the harmony but changes the voicing and may collide with the tenor, while redistributing the chord keeps the register intact and is the safer of the two fixes when the tenor has room; the diagnostic is to check every part against its range before rehearsing, not after.

questions.prompt: Two versions of a C major triad are played on a piano. Version A is C2, E2, G2 in close position. Version B is C2, G2, C3, E3, with wide gaps at the bottom and the upper voices inside an octave. Which sounds clearer, and what do the numbers say?
questions.answer: Version B, because the low register keeps wide gaps; in A the C2 and E2 fundamentals lie 17.0 Hz apart, 65.41 Hz against 82.41 Hz, narrow enough for their partials to fall inside one critical band and beat, which is heard as mud
questions.distractor: Version A, because a compact triad blends better than a spread one and a 17 Hz difference is too small for the ear to resolve at all
questions.correction: The spacing rule keeps soprano, alto and tenor within an octave of each other while allowing a larger gap between bass and tenor, and the reason given in the text is the overtone series, where intervals are wide at the bottom and narrow at the top. A close triad at C2 compresses three fundamentals into the region where the ear's filters are widest, so neighbouring partials overlap and produce roughness rather than three separate pitches. Spreading the bass to G2 and putting the third at E3 separates those partials and leaves the upper three voices close enough to blend, which is why orchestration texts advise wide spacing low, dense packing in the middle and wider spacing again at the very top.

questions.prompt: A four-bar phrase is notated at 96 beats per minute with a ritardando in the last bar down to 72. A producer enters 96 as the project tempo and finds the playback is early against the score. What are the durations, and what does the project actually need?
questions.answer: A steady reading is 10.0 s; the ritardando adds 0.377 s for a total of 10.377 s, with the last bar averaging about 83 bpm, so the project needs a tempo map with the change placed on that bar rather than a single project tempo
questions.distractor: Both readings last 10.0 s because the notation has not changed, and the project needs no tempo change since the bar count and the note values are identical
questions.correction: Tempo changes duration even though it does not change notation: at 96 beats per minute a bar is 2.5 s and four bars are 10.0 s, while a bar that slows from 96 to 72 across its four beats takes 2.877 s, so the phrase grows by 0.377 s and the bar's average tempo is 240 divided by 2.877, about 83 bpm. A single project tempo cannot represent that, which is why a tempo track or tempo map exists, and it matters differently for each material: note data follows the grid and can be re-timed by the map, while recorded audio has to be warped or the take has to be played to the map in the first place.

questions.prompt: A sixteen-bar arrangement at 92 beats per minute is to be delivered for B flat clarinet, guitar and bass guitar, with a ritardando in the final bar to 69. What is the total duration, and what does each player need in front of them?
questions.answer: About 42.13 s, since fifteen bars at 92 are 39.13 s and the final bar with the ritardando is 3.00 s; the clarinet reads a part written a major second higher than concert pitch, while guitar and bass read at sounding pitch but sound an octave below the page
questions.distractor: About 41.74 s, because the ritardando affects expression rather than time, and all three players read the concert-pitch score unchanged
questions.correction: Sixteen bars at 92 beats per minute, where a bar is 2.609 s, come to 41.739 s steady, but the final bar slows from 92 to 69 across four beats and takes 3.002 s instead of 2.609 s, so the total is 39.130 s plus 3.002 s, which is 42.132 s. Transposition is a separate question from duration: a clarinet in B flat sounds a major second below the written note, so its part is written up a major second and carries two more sharps or two fewer flats than the concert key, whereas the guitar and bass guitar are octave-transposing instruments whose parts are written at concert pitch and sound an octave lower. Sending all three players the same concert-pitch page would leave the clarinettist in the wrong key, which is the error to avoid at delivery.

questions.prompt: In a four-part phrase in F major at 84 beats per minute, the chordal seventh of C7, which is B flat, is doubled in alto and tenor and both voices then leap down to A. What is wrong, what should happen, and how long is an eight-bar phrase?
questions.answer: The seventh should appear once and resolve down by step to A, so the tenor should take G or E instead of doubling B flat; an eight-bar phrase at 84 lasts 22.857 s
questions.distractor: Doubling the seventh thickens the chord usefully and the resolution may go to any chord tone, so the only issue is that the phrase lasts 22.857 s
questions.correction: Tendency tones are single because their resolution is what the ear follows: the chordal seventh resolves down by step and the leading tone resolves up, so doubling either one produces two voices that must move the same way, which weakens the resolution and usually creates a doubled or omitted chord tone elsewhere. Doubling the root, then the fifth, and keeping the third and seventh single is the working order in four-part writing. The duration is separate arithmetic: at 84 beats per minute a beat is 0.714 s and a 4/4 bar is 2.857 s, so eight bars are 22.857 s.

questions.prompt: A melody over a bar of G7 sounds C on the downbeat, holds it while the chord changes, and then falls to B. In a second bar of G7 the same C is reached by a leap from G, accented, and resolves to B. Are these the same non-chord tone, and how do you tell?
questions.answer: They are different: the first is a 4-3 suspension because C is prepared on the same pitch and resolves down by step, and the second is an appoggiatura because it is approached by leap and resolved by step
questions.distractor: They are the same, since both are accented dissonances resolving down by step, and preparation is optional in both cases
questions.correction: Preparation is what separates the two: a suspension is approached by the same note, held as a dissonance and resolved down by step, and the textbook describes it as three stages, preparation, suspension and resolution. An appoggiatura is approached by leap and resolved by step, and it is the leap that makes it sound like an expressive leaning rather than a held note. Both are accented and both resolve downwards, which is exactly why the approach has to be checked before the label is written; the diagnostic is to look at the note before, not the note after.

questions.prompt: A learner writing a countermelody against a cantus firmus in D Dorian reaches the final unison by having both lines rise a fourth into it. Using first-species rules, what is wrong and what should the last two notes be?
questions.answer: The close must be approached by contrary motion, with one part moving 7 to 8 and the other 2 to 1, so both rising a fourth creates a direct octave and unison; the upper line should approach from C sharp or E while the lower approaches from E or C
questions.distractor: Nothing is wrong, because a unison is a perfect consonance and perfect consonances may be approached by any motion as long as the interval itself is consonant
questions.correction: The rule is the opposite of that: perfect consonances, which include unisons, fifths, octaves and twelfths, may only be approached by contrary motion, precisely to avoid direct fifths and direct octaves, while imperfect consonances may be approached freely. The exercise must also begin and end on an octave or unison, and the ending is made with one part rising 7 to 8 and the other falling 2 to 1, which is why D Dorian needs a C sharp to supply the leading tone at the close. Both lines rising a fourth into the unison produces the direct arrival the rule forbids, and the same fault is audible in four-part writing as parallel or direct octaves.

questions.prompt: A twelve-bar blues at 120 beats per minute uses one chord per bar with a quick change in bar 2, then a second version holds the tonic for the first four bars. What are the durations, and what does the change do to the phrase?
questions.answer: The form lasts 24.0 s, each bar 2.0 s; the quick change puts IV in bar 2 for 2.0 s and marks the second phrase, while holding I for four bars removes that marker and leaves the melody and the drummer to signal the phrase boundary
questions.distractor: The form lasts 24.0 s and both versions are harmonically identical, because a bar of I and a bar of IV occupy the same 2.0 s and the listener cannot tell them apart
questions.correction: Harmonic rhythm is about how long each chord lasts, and a chord substitution changes which harmony occupies that time even when the bar length is fixed, so the two versions are not identical. In the standard twelve-bar pattern the quick change to IV in bar 2 is what announces that the first four-bar group has begun rather than merely continued, and removing it is a real formal decision rather than a decoration. At 120 beats per minute a beat is 0.5 s, a bar is 2.0 s and twelve bars are 24.0 s; the arithmetic is the same in both versions, which is why the difference has to be described in function and phrasing rather than in duration.

questions.prompt: A producer stacks the same four-chord loop three ways: a single synth line; the synth plus block chords on every beat; the synth, block chords and a bass playing a separate riff. How does the texture change, and what should be checked in the arrangement?
questions.answer: Monophony becomes homorhythmic homophony and then polyphony, because the bass adds an independent line and rhythm; check that the added parts do not all attack on the same beat, since identical attacks thicken the sound without adding independence
questions.distractor: The texture is heterophonic throughout, because each added layer is a variant of the same chord loop and heterophony covers any doubling of material
questions.correction: Heterophony is specifically several simultaneous variants of one melodic line, which is not what block chords or a bass riff are; block chords moving with the melody are homophony, and the homorhythmic label applies when every voice attacks together. Once the bass has its own rhythm and contour the texture is polyphonic, and the practical consequence is that density comes from rhythmic independence as much as from the number of parts. Three layers that all hit beat one produce a thicker version of one gesture, whereas three layers with different attack points produce a texture a listener can separate, which is the check to run before adding a fourth.

questions.prompt: A horn in F is given a concert-pitch part in A major running from A3 to F sharp4. What written key and range should the horn player see, and how many sharps does that written key carry?
questions.answer: Written a perfect fifth higher, so E major from E4 to C sharp5, with four sharps
questions.distractor: Written a perfect fifth lower, so D major from D3 to B3, with two sharps
questions.correction: The direction is set by the instrument's naming note: a written C on a horn in F sounds F, a perfect fifth below, so to make the horn sound concert A the part must be written a perfect fifth above, which is E. Writing it a fifth below would produce a sounding key a fifth below the intended one, which is the mistake players hear immediately as playing in the wrong key. Transposition also moves the range, so the sounding A3 to F sharp4 becomes written E4 to C sharp5, comfortably inside the horn's working register. A major has three sharps and adding a perfect fifth adds one sharp, giving E major with four; the written key signature is always the concert signature plus the transposition interval.

questions.prompt: A tenor is asked to sustain A4 for twelve bars at 66 beats per minute in a four-part chorale texture. Using chorale-based ranges, what is the problem, how long is the passage, and what is the best fix?
questions.answer: A4 is the top of the tenor range, so twelve bars there is 43.6 s of strain; the best fix is to redistribute the chord so the alto takes the A and the tenor moves to the third or fifth below
questions.distractor: A4 is comfortable for a tenor because it lies inside the treble staff, and twelve bars at 66 beats per minute last 43.6 s with no change needed
questions.correction: The chorale ranges place the tenor from C3 to A4, so A4 is the ceiling rather than the middle, and a tessitura problem is created by duration at the limit, not by a single note. At 66 beats per minute a beat is 0.909 s and a 4/4 bar is 3.636 s, so twelve bars are 43.636 s, which is long enough for fatigue to become audible as flatness. Redistributing the chord keeps the harmony and the register of each voice, whereas transposing the whole passage down moves every part and may push the bass below its range; the check is per part against its own range before the rehearsal, not after the sound deteriorates.

questions.prompt: An arranger doubles the third of a C major triad in three octaves across a string section while leaving the root once in the bass. What is the likely result, and how should the doubling be redistributed?
questions.answer: The third, E, will dominate and the chord will stop sounding like C major in root position; double the root and the fifth instead, keep the third to one or two statements, and keep the upper voices within an octave
questions.distractor: The chord will sound fuller and more stable, because more statements of a pitch always strengthen the harmony, and the third is the note that defines the major quality
questions.correction: The third does define the quality, which is exactly why over-doubling it unbalances the chord: three statements of E against one C weights the sonority towards the mediant and can make the harmony sound like a first-inversion chord or an E chord with an added sixth. Orchestration guidance is to include all the important harmonic pitches, avoid over-doubling the third, keep wider gaps in the bass and denser packing in the middle, and return to wider spacing at the very top. Redistribution therefore means root first, fifth second, third once, with the octave doublings placed where they reinforce the fundamental rather than the mode.

questions.prompt: A pianist records a take without a click and then wants it on the grid at 88 beats per minute. What can be done to the MIDI part and what can be done to the audio, and why are the two different?
questions.answer: The MIDI part can be quantised or its tempo changed because it is note data with no inherent duration, while the audio must be warped with markers or re-recorded to the click, because a recording contains the timing as sound
questions.distractor: Both can be handled the same way, since setting the project tempo to 88 will move the audio and the MIDI together onto the grid
questions.correction: Note data stores pitch, start and length as values, so tempo is applied when the data is played and changing it re-times the part without touching the notes; MIDI is explicitly not an audio format for that reason. A recorded waveform has the performance's timing built into its samples, so fitting it to a different grid means stretching and compressing the audio with warp markers, which can introduce artefacts, or playing the take again to the click. The practical order is to decide which material is elastic and which is fixed, then to build a tempo map that follows the performance if the audio is the reference, rather than forcing the audio to a single project tempo.

questions.prompt: You must deliver a sixteen-bar piece at 92 beats per minute for B flat trumpet, cello and piano, with a written ritardando in the last bar to 69. What has to be checked for each player, and what is the total duration?
questions.answer: Trumpet reads a part written a major second higher, cello and piano read concert pitch with the cello sounding as written; check each part against its range and confirm the ritardando is marked in all three parts, for a total of about 42.13 s
questions.distractor: All three read the same concert-pitch page, and the total is 41.74 s because a ritardando is expressive rather than temporal
questions.correction: Transposition first: the trumpet in B flat sounds a major second below the page, so its part is written up a major second, which changes the key signature and the range the player sees, while the cello and piano are non-transposing and read concert pitch. Range second: each part is checked against its own working range rather than against staff position, and the cello's written range is its sounding range. Timing third: sixteen bars at 92 are 41.739 s without the ritardando, and the final bar slowing to 69 takes 3.002 s instead of 2.609 s, so the total is 42.132 s, which every part must show so the ensemble slows together rather than only the conductor.

questions.prompt: A melody uses an accented appoggiatura on the downbeat of every second bar while the harmony changes twice per bar at 104 beats per minute. What is the effect, and how long does each chord last?
questions.answer: The appoggiaturas land on strong beats where chords change, so each one is heard as a harmonic event rather than an ornament; each chord lasts about 1.154 s because a bar is 2.308 s
questions.distractor: The appoggiaturas remain melodic ornaments because they resolve by step, and each chord lasts 2.308 s because a chord lasts one bar
questions.correction: Accent and harmonic placement decide how a dissonance is heard: a non-chord tone on a weak beat is decorative, while the same tone on a downbeat, exactly where the harmony changes, is heard against the new chord and becomes an appoggiatura in the strict sense, approached by leap and resolved by step. Harmonic rhythm then controls how much time the ear has to register that clash, and at 104 beats per minute a beat is 0.577 s, a bar is 2.308 s, and two chords per bar last 1.154 s each. The two parameters interact, which is why doubling the chord rate under accented dissonances makes a phrase sound busy rather than expressive.

questions.prompt: A four-part ending in E flat major has the bass on E flat2 and the tenor a minor third above on G flat2, with soprano and alto a third apart an octave higher. Using spacing and voice-leading rules, what is the fault and the correction?
questions.answer: The bass and tenor are only a minor third apart in the lowest register, where the spacing should be widest; spread the lower voices to a fifth or octave and keep soprano, alto and tenor inside an octave, with the leading tone single and the final approached by contrary motion
questions.distractor: Nothing is wrong, because the upper three voices are within an octave and the bass may be as close to the tenor as the harmony allows
questions.correction: The rule constrains the upper three voices, soprano to alto and alto to tenor within an octave, and permits a wider gap from bass to tenor, but it does not license a minor third low down, because the overtone series is widest at the bottom and a close interval there fuses into roughness. At E flat2 the fundamental is about 77.8 Hz and G flat2 about 92.5 Hz, a difference of roughly 15 Hz, so their partials overlap and the interval sounds thick rather than clear. The correction is to open the bass spacing, keep the inner parts legal, and then check the two remaining voice-leading requirements: one statement of the leading tone and a final approached by contrary motion with 7 to 8 and 2 to 1.
